It could be really good, but not for wha tis there and the price. For like 2-3 bucks i would say "yeah i got all the fun out if it". But it feels like a very barebone incremental game with some flavor put ontop of it. I was hoping for more interesting mechanics than just "click 3 buttons" in regards to weapons, also as the game forces you to repeatadly engage in the active part to unlock the research that lets you automate it. It would have been cool if you could have like actually "assembled" a gun, even if it were just pngs you have to pull together in the right order visually to result in the complete gun. Dont misunderstand me. the visuals are great, the music is pretty good, but the core incremental part feels like it never really moves past the active part to make it run in the background, but insists to keep you engaging with the game. Either make me someone that crafts each piece with love, or a military mogul what floods the entire world with guns and maybe even moves to space and beyond. For me it feels like "just" an incremental game with not too much of its own soul. I have played a lot of incremental games and the standard-formula has become boring to me, so i was excited to maybe get some special spin on the formula, like KiWi clicker, gnorp apologue, paperclip, WAMI etc. But sadly it feels more like work than NUMBERS GO BRRR.

So i checked this out after seeing it on Dangerously Funny's channel It's a fun incremental, however i have mixed feelings about it. Despite that i will still give this a positive review. The prestige system is based on your cash per second and that makes it sometimes hard to progress. The game recommends you to prestige when you have 5 points or the game gets slow. However when it gets slow you will never reach your cash per second for the next prestige upgrade. The prestige upgrades can be picked, but not every upgrade actually helps you reach the next tier. Also you have to select them before you prestige which made me lose a prestige. The system of crafting your wares is both a strength and its weakness, while fun for the first couple of times and very unique. It can be very carpal tunnel inducing, especially with the upgrade that requires you to craft 300 pieces of something by hand to increase its automation % The game is also not very well optimised compared to other incrementals and while the dev has a anti crash version of the game and some settings to decrease the visual clutter it is still not very smooth in terms of performance. The humor and oneliners are a big plus though and are the flavor this game desperately needs, its tongue in cheeck but not overly political which is a fine balance. I say it's a decent incremental 6-7/10 but it needs some work and is best to buy during a sale, i'm not sure if its worth 10 bucks in its current state but it certainly has potential. It needs more quality of life, balancing and performance optimisation. With that in place it might end up as a 8 for me but it needs more features and depth to get anything higher.

The game turns really grindy after a short while. That is offset by buying stock. Then it turns into a afk game, because waiting for the money to come in from stocks is just the most effective way to do it midgame. At the end, when you get the option to influence the government or whatnot, the weapons become kinda viable to sell again, but you have to use them to upgrade themselves. Mid to endgame was just a slog to get through.

A fantastic incremental game that does get a tad tedious near the end. I love Military Incremental Complex for its style, the 80s music, retro Windows UI and mix of manual and idle mechanics are spot on! I adore those aspects of it it's probably one of the better games out there and some serious effort has been put into it. I love the humour added in too regarding reading the comments of the lobbyists, and how every tooltip has a little joke tossed in there as well as the fun facts when you hover over each weapon or feature, it's all fantastic! The only thing I will say, the "create 100 of x perfectly" achievements were more annoying than fun, and were hurting my hand after a while having to do such precise movements. Other than that, fantastic incremental game! from a passionate dev! Definitely check it out!

Military Incremental Complex is an idle strategy and economic simulation game that takes an unusual approach by placing players at the helm of a rapidly expanding weapons manufacturing corporation. Developed and published by Space Kraken Studios, the game blends traditional incremental mechanics with business management, political influence, and industrial expansion, creating a gameplay loop that extends well beyond simply watching numbers rise. Instead of relying solely on repetitive clicking, it gradually evolves into a sophisticated simulation where every upgrade, investment, and production decision contributes to building an enormous military enterprise. The satirical theme surrounding the military-industrial complex gives the game a distinct personality while providing an entertaining backdrop for its layered progression systems. The gameplay begins on a relatively modest scale, with players manually producing equipment and earning their first profits through direct interaction. As revenue increases, new technologies, machinery, and automated systems become available, allowing production to expand at an impressive pace. This steady evolution from manual work to a highly efficient automated operation is one of the game's biggest strengths. Every new milestone introduces fresh production opportunities, encouraging players to rethink their priorities while continuously improving efficiency. The progression rarely feels stagnant because new mechanics are introduced at a satisfying pace, rewarding both patience and strategic planning. One of the game's most engaging features is its extensive research and development system. Unlocking advanced technologies allows factories to manufacture more sophisticated equipment while improving productivity across every stage of production. Instead of offering only simple statistical upgrades, the research tree encourages meaningful choices that affect how quickly an industrial empire grows. Players must constantly decide whether to invest in immediate profit, long-term automation, or technologies that unlock entirely new production possibilities. These decisions give the game considerably more depth than many idle titles that focus almost exclusively on passive income generation. Beyond manufacturing, Military Incremental Complex expands into financial management through an integrated stock market and corporate investment system. Players can purchase shares, collect dividends, influence economic growth, and eventually gain control over competing businesses. These mechanics introduce another strategic layer that rewards thoughtful resource management rather than simply maximizing production output. Political lobbying further expands the experience by allowing players to influence government decisions, secure lucrative contracts, and increase demand for military products. These systems not only reinforce the game's satirical narrative but also diversify the gameplay, ensuring that success depends on more than simply producing larger quantities of weapons. Visually, the game adopts a clean and practical presentation that emphasizes readability over flashy effects. Production statistics, research menus, and financial information are organized clearly enough to make increasingly complex systems manageable. While the graphics remain relatively simple, they suit the genre well by prioritizing functionality during lengthy play sessions. The audio follows a similar philosophy, providing understated background music and sound effects that complement the experience without becoming repetitive or distracting. This minimalist presentation allows players to remain focused on optimization and expansion as their industrial empire grows. Another highlight is the impressive amount of content packed into the progression system. New resources, production facilities, automation upgrades, research projects, prestige mechanics, and business opportunities continuously expand the scope of the game. Rather than reaching a point where progress becomes purely numerical, players regularly unlock mechanics that significantly alter how the economy operates. This constant introduction of new objectives keeps the experience engaging over long periods and provides a strong sense of accomplishment as increasingly ambitious goals are achieved. Players who enjoy optimizing interconnected systems will likely appreciate the variety of strategic options available throughout the campaign. Despite its strengths, the game is not without drawbacks. Its satirical focus on arms manufacturing and corporate influence may not appeal to every audience, and players seeking a more traditional city builder or peaceful management simulator may find the subject matter less appealing. As production networks, investments, and research systems become increasingly interconnected, the interface can feel overwhelming, especially for newcomers unfamiliar with complex incremental games. While automation eventually reduces repetitive tasks, reaching that point requires careful planning and active management during the earlier stages, which may test the patience of players expecting a more relaxed idle experience. Military Incremental Complex ultimately delivers a surprisingly deep and rewarding blend of incremental gameplay, business simulation, and strategic management. Its combination of industrial expansion, financial systems, political influence, automation, and long-term progression elevates it above many conventional idle games. The constant stream of meaningful upgrades and evolving mechanics keeps the experience engaging from beginning to end, while its satirical premise gives the game a memorable identity. Although its complexity and unconventional theme may not suit everyone, players who enjoy building intricate economic systems and maximizing efficiency will discover an addictive and intelligently designed management experience. Rating: 8/10
